title: Startups die from co-founder breakups; solo founders die from losing hope
dek: Research shows roughly two-thirds of startup failures stem from team problems, with co-founder splits the leading killer; solo founders avoid this risk but must endure isolation and momentum loss alone.
why: For understanding an angel investor's real value and solo founders' unique survival risks; grounded in specific cases, light on generic advice.
who: Founders considering going solo or angel investors backing solo founders; also useful for entrepreneurs wanting to understand co-founder risk dynamics.
skip: The closing section on Solo Angels program enrollment (after 44 minutes) is promotional and can be skipped.

points.h: Angel investing is like collecting records: stake money, not resale value
points.body: Julian says angel investing hooked him because of the thrill of early belief—betting on a person and a company. He compares himself to a collector: acquiring vinyl records or books isn't about flipping them, which is why when a company exits he feels wistful—it means he's no longer the collector. Money was never the driver; fun, curiosity, learning come first, returns are what happen next.

points.h: Screen founders on two questions: Can they build it? Is it worth building?
points.body: Julian's framework is minimal: first, can this founder execute what's directly in front of them; second, if they do, is that thing significant—can it support a venture-scale business. He warns that some products help millions of users but don't count as venture investments; you might be building a good business but shouldn't take venture money. He adds one personal filter: would he want a text from this founder at 11pm Saturday night.

points.h: A $50 million seed locks you into an all-or-nothing outcome
points.body: Julian uses concrete numbers to show how early funding size determines the endgame: once you've taken $50 million, you need to sell the company for at least $50,000,001 before you see a dime, and that dollar has to split again by cap table. This artificially pushes the company toward binary results—massive success or zero. By contrast, even $500,000 to $1 million changes the entire math.

points.h: A $5,000 check from the right person compounds faster than intuition suggests
points.body: Julian challenges the assumption that small checks don't matter: a truly strong operator writing a $5,000 or even $1,000 check, provided dilution is small and they'll actively help, is absolutely worth taking. What matters more is momentum: several connected people each writing $5,000 introduce their networks, and you snowball into a bigger round.

points.h: Co-founder teams die from breaking up; solo founders die from giving up
points.body: Julian cites research showing roughly two-thirds of startup failures stem from people and team problems, with co-founder splits the most lethal—extremely common and destructive in co-founder teams. Solo founders sidestep this risk but face their own death: losing hope, falling into isolation, losing momentum. He quotes a founder's insight: "Rest doesn't cure burnout, momentum does"—which is why Solo Founders Program exists, to keep solo founders from being alone.

points.h: Real breakthroughs come from pulling the thread, not from pivoting
points.body: Julian tells of a student who built several working products that weren't the core answer and would have quit at good enough without deep commitment to the underlying problem. It took a full year to find the real answer; now the only serious competitor watches customers flee. Julian calls this sustained iteration pulling the thread: it looks like unrelated pivots on the surface, but each step has a line running through it. Solo founders, with no co-founder to persuade, find this easier to maintain.

points.h: Starting alone attracts co-founders of strength, not convenience
points.body: Contra's Ben bought the expensive Contra.com domain himself and built the product solo before meeting Gaius. This determination to begin alone signaled to top engineer Gaius that he was someone who acts without waiting, prompting Gaius to join as an equal rather than settle. Julian says this is solo starts' advantage: if Ben had opened by hunting a co-founder instead of building, he likely never attracts someone at Gaius's caliber.

points.h: A high school principal with no tech background shipped a millions-user product
points.body: Magic School founder Adil Khan isn't a technologist or serial entrepreneur—he's a high school principal who watched teachers get stretched thin and asked to do more. He coded the first prototype over a weekend, reached 100 users in week one, 1,000 in week two, and now teachers and administrators worldwide use it. Julian says this proves his screening standard: can this person execute (yes, product sense and distribution proven), does it matter (yes, every teacher globally needs it).

terms.def: Sustained iteration around one core problem where each step logically follows the last, rather than disconnected pivots.

terms.term: co-founder of convenience / co-founder of strength
terms.def: The first describes founders teaming up out of necessity; the second, founders each strong enough that partnering is mutual choice.
The danger that a company's survival depends entirely on one founder, so their absence would collapse the business.

facts.k: Funding that locks in all-or-nothing outcomes
